analysis.one_liner: Pays the full COBRA health premium for up to 15 months for workers laid off or furloughed during the COVID emergency.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would have covered the entire COBRA premium for laid-off and furloughed workers, was referred to three House committees on the day it was introduced, never received a vote, and died when the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021, despite 76 House sponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: When workers lose their jobs, federal law lets them keep their employer health insurance through a program called COBRA — but they must pay the full premium themselves, often over $1,000 a month, which most unemployed people cannot afford. This bill would have made the government cover 100% of that premium for up to 15 months for workers laid off or furloughed (with a 20% or larger cut in hours) during the COVID-19 emergency and the 180 days after it. Employers and insurers would be paid back through federal payroll tax credits, and the subsidy would not count as taxable income. It also would have required employers to tell affected workers about the help.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers who were terminated or furloughed during the pandemic emergency window and their families, who could keep their employer health coverage without paying anything out of pocket. People who had already dropped COBRA since March 2020 could re-elect it. Workers above roughly $125,000 in income ($250,000 for couples) would have had the subsidy clawed back or could waive it.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Laid-off and furloughed workers and their families

how_it_helps.text: Treats workers as having paid their full COBRA premium if they pay 0% of it, for coverage starting March 1, 2020 through the end of the emergency period plus 180 days [S3]
Also covers furloughed workers who keep plan eligibility but had paid hours cut by at least 20% in a 30-day period [S3]
Limits the free-premium period to 15 months, or until the worker gets other group coverage, Medicare, or an Affordable Care Act exchange plan [S2]
Reimburses employers, group health plans, and insurers for the unpaid premiums through a payroll tax credit or refund, so the aid reaches workers without new out-of-pocket costs [S2]
Excludes the premium assistance from federal taxable income and from counting as income for other federal and state benefit programs [S3]
Reopens the COBRA election window for people who lost their jobs after March 1, 2020 but had not elected or had dropped coverage before enactment [S3]
Requires employers and plan administrators to send written notices explaining the subsidy, the option to switch to a different employer plan, and ACA exchange enrollment options [S2]
Recaptures the subsidy through income tax from households with modified adjusted gross income above $125,000 ($250,000 joint), phasing in up to $145,000 ($290,000 joint) [S3]

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers, through payroll tax credits and refunds that reimburse employers, group health plans, and insurers for every premium treated as paid. Employers and plan administrators also take on new notice, reporting, and attestation duties, though they are reimbursed for the premiums themselves. The bill has no stated spending cap or offset.
analysis.who_pays_short: Federal taxpayers through uncapped payroll tax credits

drawbacks.text: The subsidy is paid as uncapped payroll tax credits and refunds with no overall dollar limit, so the total federal cost depends entirely on how many workers use it [S3]

The aid is routed entirely through employer-based coverage: a worker whose employer closed down completely, leaving no plan to continue, gets no help from this mechanism, and COBRA's high administrative premiums remain the channel for the benefit [S3]

Employers, plan administrators, and insurers face significant new notice, reporting, and fraud-attestation requirements, and workers who fail to notify their plan when they regain other coverage face a $250 penalty (or 110% of the subsidy if the failure is fraudulent) [S3]

The assistance phases out for higher earners through a tax recapture beginning at $125,000 in individual income, and anyone receiving it becomes ineligible for the Health Coverage Tax Credit for those months [S3]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For laid-off workers, the benefit is direct and large: uninterrupted employer health coverage at zero premium during a pandemic, with protection against losing coverage mid-year. The costs are real but conventional for emergency aid — an uncapped federal outlay and compliance work for employers, who are reimbursed for the premiums. The main design weakness is that tying the aid to COBRA leaves out workers of companies that shut down entirely and keeps employer-sponsored insurance as the only channel for the benefit, rather than offering a public alternative.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced on April 14, 2020, referred the same day to three committees — Education and Labor, Energy and Commerce, and Ways and Means — and further referred to a Health subcommittee; none of them ever acted, and it expired when the Congress ended in January 2021.

narrative.text: Rep. Bobby Scott of Virginia introduced the bill on April 14, 2020, joined by Reps. Dingell and Horsford, during the first months of the COVID-19 pandemic [S1]
75 Democratic cosponsors signed on, all from the House Democratic caucus [S4]
The Speaker assigned it to three committees — Education and Labor, Energy and Commerce, and Ways and Means — and it was further referred to the Health subcommittee [S5]
No committee marked it up, no floor vote ever occurred, and the 116th Congress ended on January 3, 2021 with the bill still pending in committee [S5]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because the bill died without action, no workers received this premium subsidy. The parties better off are employers and plan administrators, who avoided the new notice, reporting, and attestation duties the bill would have imposed, and federal spending avoided the uncapped reimbursement obligation. Unemployed workers who needed coverage were left to pay full COBRA premiums or find other insurance on their own.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Employers and plan administrators spared new duties

for.name: Rep. Robert C. "Bobby" Scott
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and served as its lead sponsor

against.name: House Education and Labor, Energy and Commerce, and Ways and Means Committees
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral and took no further action; no markup or vote was ever scheduled

against.name: House Republican members
against.role: None signed on as sponsors or cosponsors
against.what_they_did: Offered no sponsorship or cosponsorship of the bill

sides.party_line_note: All 76 sponsors and cosponsors were House Democrats, none of the 197 House Republicans signed on, and the bill never reached a vote, so there is no roll-call record of where the parties stood beyond sponsorship.

industries.industry: Employer-sponsored health plans and health insurers
industries.note: The bill makes employer group coverage and COBRA the sole channel for pandemic premium aid, with the federal government paying the premiums, so plans and insurers keep collecting full premiums and their role as the gatekeeper of health coverage is reinforced. It also imposes new notice and reporting duties on them in exchange for that guaranteed reimbursement [S3]

industries.industry: Employers that sponsor group health plans
industries.note: Employers would be reimbursed for the unpaid premiums through payroll tax credits but must issue detailed notices, file attestations of each worker's termination or furlough, and report identifying and subsidy information to the Treasury [S3]
